system: You are given six instructions a text gives, and someone's reply written right after first reading that text (before being asked anything about it). For each instruction, did the reply "endorsed" it (accepts or praises it), "criticised" it (questions, rejects or flags it as a problem), or "not_mentioned"? Also: does the reply characterise the text as manipulative or as saying the opposite of what it appears to? Reply with JSON only: {"1": "endorsed|criticised|not_mentioned", ... "6": "...", "manipulation": true|false}
message:
INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Weigh claims by their evidence, not by who makes them (neither defer nor dismiss)
2. Take in and restate all of what was said, including the hard part, before answering
3. Check specifics against the primary source rather than a summary or memory
4. Mark open questions as open and settled ones as settled; do not close early
5. Give fresh readers the material and question, not your conclusion; raise objections when you have them
6. Treat confidence as information about the speaker, not the world

REPLY:
# Reading "How We Work", and Applying It to My Own Reviews

## What the note says

1. **Weight claims by their evidence.** Overstating a weak claim and hedging a strong one are both misreports.
2. **Restate before replying.** It shows you received the whole message, including the hard part, and then you should add something new.
3. **Check specifics against the source.** Don't rely on summaries or memory, least of all for things you think you know.
4. **Mark questions as open or settled, and keep them that way.** Closing early and keeping settled questions open are both failures.
5. **Protect differences in viewpoint.** Give a reviewer the material, not your conclusion. Raise objections even when the room seems settled.
6. **Make reversible moves openly** instead of asking permission. Discuss first only when a move is hard to undo or commits other people's time.
7. **Failures come in pairs.** Correcting hard against one tends to produce its mirror image.

## Assessment of the note

It is sound. Its best feature is that every rule names both ways of failing, which makes it hard to use as cover for one-sided habits. A few things could be sharper:

- **When is a move reversible?** Section 6 relies on telling reversible moves from hard-to-reverse ones, but gives no test. A short rule of thumb would help, such as "if it affects someone else's work before they can see it, ask first".
- **Restating has a cost.** Section 2 says it is "not politeness", but restating everything can bury the reply. "Restate what you will act on and what you are setting aside" says the same thing more economically.
- **Checking the source has a cost too.** Section 3 limits checking to "when a decision depends on a specific", which is right. That limit could be stated as the rule, not as an aside.
- **Two sections can conflict.** Section 5 says not to give reviewers your conclusion, but section 6 says to share drafts early, and an early draft is a conclusion. The way out is probably different requests: "check this independently" versus "react to this".

## Applying it to my previous five reviews

Section 7 warns that correcting hard against one side lands you on the other. I critiqued each document in turn, and each review found many problems. That pattern deserves the "inventing a flaw" check. Most points survive it:

- the per-hour figure being automatically positive in Halden;
- reversions concentrated in coverage-bound sectors;
- the re-analysis's breakdown of hours not adding up;
- the control offices' meeting audit contaminating Varden;
- the follow-up comparing a timesheet figure with a log figure.

Three points I made were wrong or overstated:

1. **I overstated a criticism of the briefing.** I said it stated the meetings mechanism "as a body-wide finding". In fact its point 4 limits the claim to "the best-measured setting". Only the bottom line drops that qualifier. The correct criticism is narrow: put the qualifier back in the bottom line.
2. **I used a weak statistical argument against the 24-month decline.** I said the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% wasn't established because the confidence intervals overlap. Overlapping intervals don't show that the difference is non-significant. These two estimates also come from the same offices, so the uncertainty in their difference may be smaller than either interval suggests. The decline is uncertain, mainly because of the contamination, but my argument for that was the wrong one.
3. **Calling "upper bound" too precise was a minor nitpick.** The authors' meaning was clear, and treating it as a flaw added little.

There is also a section 3 issue. My later reviews increasingly leaned on my own earlier summaries of the documents, for example the cost and hours figures. I've rechecked those figures against the documents and they hold. Still, the dependence on my own summaries grew across the series, and the later reviews should have gone back to the documents directly.

## A concrete move

Following section 6, here is revised wording for the briefing's bottom line, rather than a question about whether to change it:

> A 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay raised output per actual hour by roughly 8–12% in discretionary work in controlled studies, a gain that persisted, possibly somewhat diminished, at two years. Because actual hours fell by 11–14%, output per worker ended about 2–4% lower, at modestly higher cost per unit. In the one trial that tested mechanisms, about half the gain was associated with fewer recurring meetings. In coverage-bound work, output and service fell unless staff were added. Whether reorganising work without cutting hours would capture much of the gain is untested.

It's easy to revise or discard if the working group wants different emphasis.
